source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.

Amidst this retail ritual, the tally rings its total—there’s a pause to query loyalty status—and the dance of bagging concludes, leaving each transaction neatly sealed. She hands over her card, and as it slides into the slot, her purchase is complete; in that moment, her gaze meets his across the counter, an unspoken dialogue between shopper and attendant in this daily theatre of commerce. They part ways then, she with her bags, he with a nod towards the next awaiting their turn in line, each a piece in the grand tableau of checkout efficiency.

Here each interaction was measured by tokens scanned and transactions completed with efficiency, yet even in such a structured environment, moments of friction could arise over inches of standing room. As items piled up on the conveyor belt, she felt a nudge from behind her; it whispered an urgency to move along, but here the rhythm dictated its pace, steady and unyielding. In these aisles where time marched with precision, every step was accounted for, yet it couldn't prevent the brief skirmishes over mere inches of shared space.
